title: Comparisons of the Distributions for One Quantitative Variable
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 1.9 Comparisons of the Distributions for One Quantitative Variable
intro: Compare distributions directly and use z-scores to compare relative positions within different reference groups.

moments.title: Compare full distributions
moments.text: Compare center, spread, shape, and unusual features.

moments.title: Boxplot comparisons
moments.text: Compare median and IQR while recognizing what is not shown.

moments.title: Use comparative sentences
moments.text: Say which group has the larger center or greater spread.

moments.title: Standardized scores
moments.text: Express a value's displacement in standard-deviation units.

moments.title: The z-score formula
moments.text: Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation.

moments.title: Interpret the sign
moments.text: A negative score is below the mean; a positive score is above it.

moments.title: Relative position
moments.text: Compare individuals relative to their own distributions.

moments.title: A raw score needs a reference
moments.text: The same score can have different z-scores in different classes.

moments.title: Score of 78
moments.text: A score of 78 with mean 80 and SD 5 is slightly below average.

cards.name: Compare like with like
cards.text: Use the same variable and units, and pair median with median or mean with mean.

cards.name: Compare directly
cards.text: State higher or lower center and greater or smaller spread, supported by values.

cards.name: Standardize
cards.text: Subtract the reference mean and divide by the reference SD.

cards.name: Interpret relative performance
cards.text: A higher z-score means a higher relative value; whether that is better depends on context.

questions.obj: Compare the same score in different classes
questions.q: In the video, a score of 78 is compared with a class mean of 80 and SD 5, and with another class mean of 70 and SD 12. Calculate and interpret both z-scores.

work.text: Use the first class's mean and SD.
Use the second class's mean and SD.
The first score is 0.4 SD below its class mean. The second is about 0.667 SD above its class mean.

questions.answer: 78 has the higher relative position in the second class, even though the raw score is the same.

traps.title: Two separate descriptions
traps.weak: A has median 20. B has median 30.
traps.better: B has the higher median: 30 minutes compared with 20 minutes for A.

traps.title: A percentile from a z-score
traps.weak: A z-score of 1 means the 84th percentile for any data.
traps.better: A z-score of 1 means one SD above the mean. A percentile requires distributional information.

traps.title: Reversed subtraction
traps.weak: Subtract the score from the mean.
traps.better: Subtract the mean from the score, then divide by SD.

traps.title: Higher means better
traps.weak: The largest z-score always represents the best result.
traps.better: Higher is better for some outcomes, but lower is better for outcomes such as completion time.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: Z-scores can be calculated without a normal model. Statements about most observations being within one, two, or three SDs need distributional qualifications.

questions.stem: A time of 42 minutes is recorded in a population with mean 50 and SD 4 minutes. What is its z-score?
why: The sign must be negative because 42 is below 50.

opts: B has a higher median and a smaller IQR than A
why: This says nothing about the distributions.
It compares matching measures of center and spread.
This does not compare statistical features.

questions.stem: Rae has z=1.4 in a speed test; Sol has z=0.9 in a different speed test. Which follows?
opts: Rae's speed is farther above its reference mean in SD units
Rae must have the larger raw speed
Rae must be at the 90th percentile
The two tests have equal SDs
why: Raw speeds depend on different means and SDs.
Standardizing does not imply equal original SDs.

questions.stem: Which is required to calculate a z-score?
opts: A reference mean and a positive SD
why: Normality is not needed for the calculation.
These are not the values in the z formula.
The SD must be positive to divide by it.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: Route A has median travel time 32 minutes and IQR 8 minutes. Route B has median 38 minutes and IQR 5 minutes. For a different comparison, population means and SDs are A: 34 and 4 minutes; B: 40 and 6 minutes.
parts: (a) Compare typical travel time and the middle-half variability.
(b) Find the z-score of a 30-minute journey on each route.
(c) Which 30-minute journey is relatively faster, and why does a z-score not give an exact percentile here?
sample: (a) Route A has the shorter typical time, with median 32 versus 38 minutes. Route B has the less variable middle half, with IQR 5 versus 8 minutes.

(c) The B journey is relatively faster because it is farther below its route's mean in SD units. The population distribution shapes are not given, so these z-scores do not determine exact percentiles.
checklist: Explains why the lower standardized time is relatively faster.
